newsitem.title: USA: Downgrade may hurt new sales at Prudential unit.
newsitem.headline: Downgrade may hurt new sales at Prudential unit.

text.p: Prudential Insurance Co of America's property and casualty business may have a tougher time making new sales after a downgrade of its financial strength rating by insurance rating agency A.M. Best.
The action also may reflect a new, tougher stance by A.M. Best in its rating of property and casualty companies.
The financial strength ratings, which measure an insurer's ability to pay claims, are used by agents, brokers and consumers when deciding where to place their business, analysts said.

A.M. Best cut its rating on Prudential Property and Casualty Insurance Co and its three reinsured affiliates to B++ from A-, citing poor operating earnings, earnings volatility and above-average catastrophe risk.

Salomon Brothers analyst Michael Smith said he expects A.M. Best to downgrade the ratings of other property and casualty companies in the coming months because of concern about excessive catastrophe exposure.
"That is clearly a wake-up call to the rest of the industry that you've got to get your (catastrophic risk) exposures down," Smith said.

Smith said the agency appears to be expressing concern that insurance companies with excessive catastrophe exposures are going to be unstable in their markets, creating insurance availability and pricing problems.
"What Best wants and everyone wants is stable companies that don't pull out of markets," Smith said.
Best's concern about the industry's catastrophe exposures was signalled in similar moves earlier this year, Smith said.
In September, Best assigned Allstate Corp's Allstate Floridian Insurance Co an initial B++ rating and in May lowered State Farm Fire & Casualty Co to A from A+.
The downgrade may spur Prudential to take additional actions to resolve the rating agency's concerns, industry sources said.
They said the downgrade may prompt Prudential to infuse more capital into the company or consider a possible sale of the business.
But a Prudential spokesman said the business was not for sale. In addition, he said, Prudential, disagreed with Best's action, saying it has already taken steps to improve the business.
Prudential said it hired a new president for the unit in January and said it has already made substantial progress in trimming its exposure to catastrophes in California, Florida and the Northeast.
Indeed, A.M. Best noted those actions and acknowledged Prudential's strong financial backing of the property and casualty business.

Some analysts said they did not believe the downgrade would have much of an impact on Prudential's property and casualty insurance sales, saying retail customers usually don't pay much attention to the ratings.
Prudential's property and casualty business sells mostly personal auto and homeowners' insurance to individual consumers.
Large commercial buyers, who want to be sure that the insurer will be around years later to pay claims, watch ratings very closely.
But Salomon's Smith said all consumers have become increasingly concerned about the solvency of their insurers.
"Consumers and commercial buyers are more and more sensitive to the stability of their insurance company," Smith said. "I've got to believe a B double plus (rating) is a severe penalty," he said.
"I don't care if you're a personal lines or commercial lines company. You don't want to incur a B rating."
